arrival.label: Before you enter
paragraphs: We know who he would become.
As you enter, set that knowledge aside.

halls.title: Origins and Uncertainty
paragraphs: Vincent’s story begins in a pastor’s household in the Netherlands. School took him away from home. Work carried him to other cities, where he encountered pictures, books, new acquaintances and the practical demands of earning a living.

In London, his letters describe a room he enjoyed, walks through the city and seeds planted in a garden. Religious work later brought him into the mining communities of the Borinage. His plans changed, and the question of how to make a useful life remained.

The opening film follows these years. As you move towards the drawings, you meet Vincent at the beginning of another undertaking. In 1880, he decided to become an artist. Learning how would occupy the years ahead.

halls.title: Earth and Labour
paragraphs: A figure bends over the ground. A woman prepares food. People gather around a table at the end of a working day.

Vincent returned to such subjects throughout his early years as an artist. In Etten, The Hague, Drenthe and Nuenen, he studied working people and the spaces in which ordinary life unfolded. His letters discuss models, materials, money and the difficulties of drawing what he saw.
Family relationships and attempts to establish a household formed part of these years. Painting gradually became the work around which he organised his life.
Spend time with the figures in this room. Follow the position of a hand, the weight of a body and the objects placed within reach. These details held his attention through repeated study.

halls.title: The Paris Transformation
paragraphs: In 1886, Vincent arrived in Paris and moved in with Theo. The brothers could now share the daily conversations that distance had previously carried into their letters.

The city brought Vincent into contact with artists, exhibitions and unfamiliar approaches to painting. He studied Japanese prints, experimented with colour and painted flowers, streets and his own face. His surroundings offered a continuing supply of subjects and ideas.
Across this room, changes emerge from one work to another. Colours grow brighter. Brushmarks take different forms. Compositions reveal ideas he was exploring.
Imagine the activity surrounding these paintings: visits, conversations, pictures examined closely and another canvas begun. His practice developed within that exchange.

halls.title: Arles: Toward the Sun
paragraphs: Vincent arrived in Arles in February 1888. As the seasons changed, he painted blossoming orchards, wheatfields and the streets of the town. He also turned his attention to cafés, bedrooms and people he came to know.
His letters describe plans for a shared studio in the south. He rented the Yellow House and prepared rooms where another artist could live and work. Paintings became part of those preparations.
Walk through this gallery as a place taking shape around him. The countryside offered subjects, the house gave structure to his plans, and acquaintances entered his pictures.
During these months, Vincent was working towards a daily life in which painting and companionship could grow together.

halls.title: Companionship and Crisis
paragraphs: Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888. The Yellow House became a shared household and workplace. The two artists painted, discussed their methods and made portraits of people around them.

Living together brought their different expectations into daily contact. Tensions developed, and their collaboration ended during the crisis of December. Vincent received hospital care and returned to painting as his condition allowed.
This room follows the relationship and the months that came after it. Paintings, letters and accounts of the ear injury preserve different kinds of evidence. Some details remain unresolved.
Take time with the aftermath. Correspondence continued, practical questions needed attention, and Vincent considered where he could live and work with support.

halls.title: Saint-Rémy: Inner Skies
paragraphs: In May 1889, Vincent entered Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy. His daily surroundings included a room, hospital corridors, a garden and views towards the nearby countryside.

When he was able to work, he gave sustained attention to these places. Irises, olive trees, cypresses and fields became subjects for painting. Prints after artists he admired offered material he could work from indoors. Episodes of illness interrupted this activity.
Move slowly among the works gathered here. Notice how a familiar subject changes across several pictures, and how much can be explored within a limited setting.
His letters record concerns about his health alongside decisions about pictures, colours and future plans. Painting remained an important part of his days.

halls.title: Auvers: The Final Months
paragraphs: Vincent arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise on 20 May 1890. He took lodgings at the Ravoux inn and began exploring his surroundings through painting. In an early letter to Theo and Jo, he described studies of thatched roofs and a field of flowering peas, with wheat in the foreground. He asked for canvas or drawing paper so that he could keep working.

By early June, he was painting Dr Gachet’s portrait and making studies in the doctor’s garden. He wrote about getting up early, the materials he needed and the possibility of Theo, Jo and their young son coming to stay. There were paintings to make, supplies to arrange and people he hoped to see.

The portraits, village views and wide landscapes in this room bring us into the activity of those weeks. Across them, Vincent continued to explore colour, brushwork and the shape of the canvas. His work in Auvers forms a concentrated period of experimentation within his artistic life.

Vincent died on 29 July 1890, two days after sustaining a gunshot wound. The final section of this gallery follows those days through documents, recollections and later research. It also considers the different explanations proposed for the shooting, with their sources and limitations made visible.

As you move through the room, give time to the people, places and paintings that occupied him. Beyond this gallery, Afterlife follows the people who preserved his work and the encounters it made possible.

halls.title: Afterlife
halls.subtitle: What His Work Set in Motion
halls.tourLead: Vincent’s paintings and letters passed into the care of others. Through exhibitions and publication, they reached new audiences. Artists explored their possibilities; musicians and filmmakers responded in their own forms. This gallery follows those encounters and invites you to consider your own.
paragraphs: Vincent’s paintings and letters passed into the care of others. Through exhibitions and publication, they reached new audiences. Artists explored their possibilities; musicians and filmmakers responded in their own forms. This gallery follows those encounters and invites you to consider your own.

Begin with the people who cared for the collection. Jo van Gogh-Bonger’s exhibition and editorial work, and Vincent Willem’s later stewardship, helped paintings and letters reach future viewers. The surviving photographs, catalogues and books let you follow that work through particular objects.

Then follow a museum-curated connection to later painting, a song by Don McLean and an imagined encounter in Akira Kurosawa’s cinema. These are responses to Vincent’s work, not new evidence about his life. His story now reaches you. As you leave, what will you carry with you from Vincent’s life?
